utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. Today is Wednesday, 27th of January, 2010. I would like to welcome everyone in the courtroom, including the accused, the counsels, the witness, Mr. Stringer, Mr. Kruger, and their fellow workers, as well as everybody else helping us in the courtroom. We're going to carry on with the cross-examination with Mr. Kruger. Mr. Kruger, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. Good morning to everybody in and around the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Mr. Jasak, good morning to you. Now, Mr. Jasak, I'm moving on to a new topic now, and I'm going to explore with you the question whether the attack by the Muslims on the 30th of June, 1993, came as a surprise to the HVO. Now, the first question that I want to ask you: Can you just confirm once again that between the 9th of May, 1993, and the 30th of June, 1993, is it so that the HVO and the ABiH were still at all times allies against the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the 19th of May to the 30th of June, the BH Army and the HVO were allies in the Defence against the Serbs --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 9th of May.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- facing the Army of Republika Srpska. The 30th of June was a surprise for the military leaders, although according to our assessments, there were indications that something like that could happen. But it was, nonetheless, a surprise, and that because after the 9th of May, 1993, a significant portion of Muslims left the HVO voluntarily, without any problems, and those who remained in the units thought -- well, their commanders thought that they sincerely wanted to fight with the HVO against the Army of Republika Srpska, particularly since they were there from the very beginning, that is to say, from 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, that confirms what you've told previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, Your Honour, for the next three documents, if we can move into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, earlier you confirmed that between 9 May and 30 June 1993, the HVO and the ABiH were at all times still allies against the Serbs. Now, let's have a look at what General Petkovic and the HVO is busy with during this period. And now let's have a look at -- the next exhibit is P02910. It's towards the first part of your binder, about the seventh or the eighth document. P02910. Now, sir, this document - it is in evidence - is a request by Colonel Zeljko Siljeg, and it's dated the 22nd of June, 1993. And it's to the Herceg Stjepan Brigade in Kostajnica, and it says: "Request immediately from XY to open fire at Konjic and Celebici at 4.30." The XY side, that refers to the Serbs, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said it about a previous document. I've not seen this before. I don't know what this is about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: So you confirm that "XY" refers to the Serbs; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what it refers to in here. Earlier on, when you asked me about another XY, my answer was affirmative. It is possible that the same applies here, but I've not seen the document before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, isn't it so that in that area, Konjic and Celebici, at least then, that the Serbs and the HVO had a cooperative kind of understanding, at least, at the time when the HVO was allied with the Muslims against those same Serbs?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as Konjic is concerned, we know that some contacts were made among locals from the area, those who were in Turija, Zabrdje, Zaslivlje, and who saved the local Serbs during the complete ethnic cleansing that had taken place during the previous month, starting with the 23rd March, 1993, which was followed by a large-scale offensive that was launched on the 13th of April. And that's when the ethnic cleansing of all the area started and all non-Muslims were expelled. At that time, they received a certain number of Serbs, they saved their lives. Turija, Zabrdje, and Zaslivlje politicians received Serbs, and through them they established contacts in the area because --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: I have to interrupt you. It's all very interesting, but I wasn't looking for an explanation. I was simply asking: Isn't it so that there was a cooperative agreement between the Serbs and the Croats in that area at that time, or a cooperative arrangement?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, I don't know. I don't think that there was a contact between the top of the HVO and the Serbs at the time when this was written. This is a local level, and reference is made to the Herceg Stjepan Brigade in Kostajnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let's move to the next document. But before moving to it, just for the context in which this question is -- the questioning is going to come, we have now seen that -- we've seen whether you agree with it or not, information that would indicate --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as this document is concerned, I have a question of a technical nature and a military nature. Seemingly, Colonel Siljeg is asking the Herceg Stjepan Brigade to contact XY to open fire at Konjic and Celebici at 4.30. A good investigation would have checked the military documents of the VRS and would have checked whether any request had been sent by the HVO. Then proof would have been established. I'm addressing myself to you now, as a military man. When a request is made by someone, is there a written trace of this, in military terms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know how the possible requests went. There is a paper trail here about Siljeg's request from a brigade, but apparently all this was happening in Konjic, where the situation was difficult. I don't know what the Herceg Stjepan Brigade in Kostajnica had and what Turija and Zabrdje and Zaslivlje had, how they communicated, whether they had radio communication. I don't know. This is a request which went via the brigade. That was a small part that still remained outside of the complete control of the Muslims at the time, because if you look at the entire period when, for over a month, perhaps 40 days or so, I don't know how many days exactly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall pick up my question at the other end. Let's imagine that the Serbs are asking something from the HVO. Would the HVO have written something down in a log-book, Have received such and such a time, such and such a date, a specific request? Would you have a paper trail of such a request?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know nothing about such requests.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, please listen to my question. Please listen. This is something I am assuming. If the Serbs -- if the Serbs had asked something from the HVO, would there be a paper trail of this at the HVO of the request and of the follow-up to the request?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I suppose that requests had to be recorded and acted upon. Otherwise, how would anybody know that things had been requested?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's all I wanted to know. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, let's turn to Exhibit -- it's two documents further on in your binder, Exhibit P02919. 2919. Now, sir, this is a protest from Commander Rasim Delic, and it's addressed to Mr. Milivoj Petkovic, and it's dated the 23rd of June, 1993. It says: "Dear sir. By signing the accord on the cessation of the conflicts in Bosnia and Herzegovina between the units of the HVO and units of the Army of RBiH on 10 June 1993 in Kiseljak, and the protocol about Bosnia and Herzegovina on 15 June 1993 in Sarajevo Airport, we again confirmed the accord from Medjugorje and the intention to eliminate the basic causes of conflict between the HVO and the Army of RBiH. That accord includes regulations on deliberation of all captives. The fact that the Croatian Defence Council is hindering the implementation of that accord causes doubts not only in the honesty of the intentions when signing the accord, but also the possibility of its further implementation." And if we go to the end of the document, the final paragraph, it says: "Since these facts cause serious doubts in the readiness of the HVO to honestly and without reservations give their contributions to the accord implementation, we hereby protest against such behaviour, and we demand strict respect of the obligations that you have taken upon signing the accord." Did you know about this protest or this document? Did you ever see it?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've never seen this document before, but I did know that what they did at the time they ascribed to the Croatian Defence Council. So they did not respect -- that is to say, the BH Army did not respect what was signed, and then accused the HVO to gain in time for some of their actions. They would get together, discuss the matter, and then -- because linked to Travnik --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I must object to this, that the witness is being prompted from General Praljak from the bench. I must object, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me. Mr. President, I apologise for the intervention. We've been looking at some of the tape of some of the chatter that's been coming from the accused over the course of proceedings this week, and it's our view that there is coaching that's taking place. There have been situations where we think answers are being suggested to the witness, and we ask the Trial Chamber to be vigilant about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please wait, Ms. Alaburic. This is an objection that hasn't got to do with the substance of the case or with the position of Judges on one or the other part of the indictment, but it has to do with the behaviour of General Praljak. And the Prosecution has pointed out that, according to them, the witness seems to be prompted by General Praljak when answering, or under the influence of General Praljak. So it is totally unacceptable for an accused to intervene when a question is put to a witness and when the witness is to answer this question. I have always challenged this type of behaviour, especially when some counsels are speaking. So the person putting the question has to let be, and the witness has to also be in a position to answer freely. So, General Praljak, I would like to know whether you intervened to coach the witness, because this accusation is very serious. Please, General Praljak, can you answer? THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I did not say anything to the witness, not once, but I did say to General Petkovic, which might have been -- well, might have been picked up by the microphone. I did say to him that a statement by Delic of this kind relates precisely to the situation when they took control of Travnik and Kakanj, because we've become ill from all this. A very complicated situation, and then details are extracted which have nothing to do with the truth. They took Travnik and Kakanj, and then they accused the HVO, in an underhand manner. And I said that I was upset by this to Mr. Petkovic, but I never said anything to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, you say that you spoke to General Petkovic, but when saying this it can be heard by the witness, and I'm sure it was heard by the witness and by the Prosecutor. I was not listening, because I was looking at the documents and I did not look at what was going on. And given that I do not speak your language, I would not have understood what you said, anyway. But in future, please refrain from speaking to your fellow accused. So as I was saying, please avoid to take the floor. In fact, you should actually be positioned in such a way that you cannot really talk to General Petkovic. If Mr. Pusic was between the two of you, this would avoid this sort of problem in the future. Yes, Ms. Alaburic. I don't know what you wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your permission, may I just respond to the statement made by my learned friend Mr. Stringer, because it does not relate just to General Praljak, but it relates to the Defence witness, General Petkovic -- or, rather, General Petkovic's witness, Mr. Jasak. I do understand the efforts made by the Prosecution at great length to discredit this witness, and one of the ways in which they've been trying to do this -- that Mr. Kruger tried to do this ever since yesterday is to say that the witness is answering and that he is being coached by someone in the ranks of the accused. I think that is completely unacceptable. And as for looking at the tape to establish whether the witness answered the questions posed straightaway or not or whether he asked for an expected -- any suggestions from anybody in the courtroom, I suggest that we all look at the tapes together, because then we'll be able to see that the witness responded straightaway, without holding any consultations with anybody, because this witness does not need to consult anybody when providing his answers. And everybody looking at him and weighing up his answers can come to the same conclusion, and that is why I think Mr. Stringer's objection, referring to having examined the tapes and then determining whether the witness is behaving in one way or another, is incorrect, and I think that Mr. Stringer ought to apologise to the witness for his observations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, you're mainly involved with this. As I said, I was looking at the document, but I was also looking at you, and most of the time you seem to be looking towards Mr. Kruger. So it seems that you were not looking at General Praljak. But you are testifying under oath, and so you have to tell the truth. So I would like to know whether you heard what General Praljak said to General Petkovic, or were you mainly concerned by the question or by the document or by the screen, and therefore you didn't hear anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I was dealing with what was on the screen and what was here, too, but I did hear something. I heard General Praljak speaking, but I didn't need General Praljak to tell me anything, because I said that I'd never seen this document before, but I do know -- I'm aware of the contents. So they were accusing the HVO of something that they, themselves, did not respect. They signed something, but they did not abide by what they had signed. So that's it. But I didn't hear that from General Praljak, certainly not. And I suggest if the Prosecutor thinks that suggestions are coming from the accused, they could put up a screen. I can't monitor my actions and know whether I'm turning to the left or right. So why don't they put up a screen, and then we'll exclude that possibility. And I don't need anybody to tell me what my replies should be. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I wasn't in court yesterday. I made no comments before that. I just dealt with some of my affairs here exclusively, and I just said what I said a moment ago to General Petkovic. I never wielded any influence on the witness, nor is it my concern -- well, yes, at this point in time, because when this letter was written, 40.000 Croats were expelled from Kakanj and Travnik and were roaming around some hills. So this went on for four years, and you haven't tried to find the truth. But tricks are being devised, and that is something I have been saying here from the very beginning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, you have to keep yourself together. When a witness testifies, he is the only one speaking. You are not allowed to say anything. You can write notes to your counsels, and, in fact, we have someone in this courtroom that can help you to do so, but that's the only thing that you can do, because if you say anything, if those words are heard in the courtroom, we may think that you are expressing a view which could influence the witness. This is the main issue at stake here, and this is why, when counsels are raising objections, I would say please let the witness answer first. So if I'm saying that to counsels, it's even more valid for you. So please keep quiet and let the Prosecutor ask questions, and let the witness answer. And if you're not happy with the answers, then you can tell your counsel that he made a mistake. You can do it, but you have to do it through notes, in order for you to have a dialogue between you and your counsel, because your counsel can then raise an objection, if this objection is dealing with a mistake. But if it's in the substance, of course, then you need to have Judges taking a position, and I'm against this because I cannot actually have a position on some issues at the moment, issues that are dealing with the direct responsibility or liability of the accused. It would mean that they are guilty or they are innocent, and I have not reached that stage yet in this trial. So this is why, for some objections, I do not say anything, but for other objections, such as the one coming from Mr. Kruger, that are perfectly legitimate, and in which case, I do intervene. Now, if my colleagues, when they have objections, want to take the floor, they can also take the floor, but it is going to be their responsibility. Mr. Kruger, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I just ask a question, just a point of information. The -- Mr. Stringer expressed his objection, but it's -- can we be clear, it's not suggested, is it, and if it is, it's helpful to know, that the witness has ever been able to hear a specific suggestion, because, after all, the accused -- I want to make this point: General Praljak and General Petkovic are -- as long as it's not disruptive, they are perfectly entitled to discuss matters between themselves where they sit. They are two gentlemen on trial for very serious crimes, and if it is helpful to them, discreetly and not disruptively, to discuss things, then that's a freedom that they absolutely must have. But unless their microphones get turned on when they do that, I'm not clear at the moment whether it's suggested that it's actually possible that the witness, sitting there with the earphones on his ears, could ever actually hear anything. Can I just be clear about what is being suggested, because -- in fact, if I could just add this: Ms. Alaburic's suggestion that, not necessarily in open court, but we might at some point look together at these tapes to see what it is that's being suggested by way of coaching this witness is a sensible, practical suggestion, because we have a very strong interest on General Petkovic's behalf in ensuring that there is no doubt about this witness's evidence and no seeds of doubt are sown in this particular way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I am, of course, in a double role now as Judge and witness, and I must say I am hard of hearing, I have the earphones, but I have heard words from the bench of the accused through all this. Of course, I couldn't have understood, but I think the incident is not as completely harmless. I have several times, today and over the last days, heard words being spoken. That is not the discretion which you rightly demand.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: To some extent, that's helpful, Your Honours. To some extent, that answers my question. Well, it partly answers my question. It deals -- I'm slightly surprised that it is technically possible for words from the accused's bench, when their microphones are not on, to actually reach the witness's ears. But if it happens, if it's capable of happening, then, well, it's technically possible. There is, therefore, my question whether Mr. Stringer is suggesting that actually that method of communication has actually been achieved. So that is he saying that the witness has actually heard words, as opposed to gestures or some sort --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, let me interrupt you, because I would like to quote on the screen and it is now disappearing: "I agree with you that they are --" I mean, "the accused have the right to discuss amongst themselves issues," as you put it, "discreetly and not disruptively." This one, what you have said, that's correct. Nobody denies that right from the accused to talk about issues, but, as you put it, discreetly and not disruptively. Now, frankly, I also would like to say what also was already mentioned by Judge Trechsel and by others, that many times we have been listening to noises, to discussion, et cetera. Probably it is due to the rather strong voice by General Praljak, et cetera. I admit that. But on the other hand, I believe that in the future they have to really behave in a way that is not disruptive as far as our proceedings are concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm not going to quarrel with any of that, with respect. Part of my comment was provoked by some slight concern about what the President said at page 25, lines 7 to 9: "You should actually be positioned in such a way that you cannot really talk to General Petkovic if Mr. Pusic was between the two of you," because that would remove what I've said and what Your Honour Judge Prandler has specifically just agreed is a freedom that the accused should have. If the -- the accused, no doubt, are registering in the course of this discussion the technical position that -- following what Judge Trechsel said, that what they say might be apparently capable of being heard and understood by a witness in his own language, so no doubt their discretion in future ought to take account of that possibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, it is a matter of keeping the discretion, keeping the voices down. I feel disturbed. I hear talking back there, and I feel disturbed, and that is not correct. And if it is necessary to separate two accused because they disrupt, that is absolutely legitimate, because the right to communicate cannot lead to disrupting the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I say that -- [Overlapping speakers] ... Sorry. May I say, Your Honour, that what I just said immediately before Your Honour spoke is, with respect, entirely consistent with that. I'm suggesting that everything that is being said, one hopes and trusts, naturally, will have been registered by all concerned so that they can see that that freedom, which they should have, should be exercised in a way that does not have any possible result. I'm not saying -- I'm not accepting that that has happened. I just don't know. I'm not a witness on this. But for the future, we want, of course, them to have that freedom, but we don't want any sort of disruption. But whether there has, in fact, been the result that Mr. Stringer suggests, well, Your Honour, I don't know. I'm not a witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Coric, you stood up. Do you want to take the floor? THE ACCUSED CORIC: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I was not here in the courtroom when what happened took place, so I can't really talk about the matter, but what I have heard since I re-entered the courtroom over the past two or three minutes, you're speaking only of the consequences. You're not speaking about the causes, why we have been brought into this position to sit one beside the other, and not sitting with our Defence teams, as you proposed, Judge Antonetti, at the beginning. Now, whether by some Statute or other regulation regulated, whether the accused sitting in this position have the right to communicate, and how to communicate, and so on and so forth, so everything that is happening here is just the consequence, the result, and not the cause. Now, the second point. The time of my Defence case is coming up, and I'm going to address the Trial Chamber with a request, or, rather, my Defence counsel will, that during my Defence case some matters are done because they are impeding my Defence and the fair conduct of this trial, and are impeding ultimately my health. So I think it is essential, vital, in what position we are when we present our views and positions. You're talking about your problems, but I'd like you to hear what our problems are. Perhaps I'm bothered by other people talking, the people next to me, or perhaps they're bothered by my comments. So these are questions that should have been ruled upon at the beginning of this trial, whereas we're dealing with it far into the trial. So we're going to write a written request that when my Defence case comes up, that certain things be established.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Prlic. THE ACCUSED PRLIC: [Interpretation] One sentence: I think that we've exaggerated and gone on for too long with this topic. The trial has been going on for four years now, and now suddenly that somebody can gain the impression that somebody is behaving in a wild manner is not the case. I consider that it's just a technical matter that we're dealing with. I very often hear the Defence counsel and the Judges for only one reason, because the person speaking does not take off his head-sets and can't control the volume of his own voice. I've been sitting here for four years, and I don't have the impression that anybody is trying to influence the trial in any improper way at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm entitled to speak at some point, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have just one sentence which will follow on to what Mr. Prlic has just said. So might I be allowed to state what I wanted, and then Mr. Stringer can react to the entirety of what is being said? Mr. Prlic has just said precisely what I was going to say, that with respect to this particular witness, nothing different happened from what has been happening here in this courtroom for four years. And the endeavours of the Prosecution for the second witness -- week now to discredit this witness at any price I consider to be a great compliment to this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, maybe it is because the trial's lasted so long that there's a certain familiarity that creeps into the proceedings. But the fact is that people who don't have the floor in this courtroom talk too loud, and it's something I've raised in the past, whether it's other counsel or the accused. When you're in the courtroom and you don't have the floor, if you've got something to say, you whisper, you talk like you're in church, and nobody seems to do that in this courtroom. Getting to the point raised by Mr. Stewart, whether or not coaching is going on, I can assure Mr. Stewart and the Trial Chamber that it is highly distracting to us all the way over here, because we can hear what's being said over there. We can't understand it, which makes it worse, because the microphones are not on and what's being said is not in the record, but it's highly distracting, even apart from whether there is coaching going on. And it's impolite. And it's discourteous to whoever has the floor at that time. Now, whether General Praljak or any of the other accused are intending to coach the witness, the fact is that whether they're talking to the witness or whether they're talking among themselves, when they're talking to each other in advance of an answer that's to come from the witness, it can have the effect of coaching, and that's how we interpret it. And so that's really all I've got to say. I think that if we could go back to perhaps where we were at the beginning of the trial - I wasn't here then, but the accused were, and I bet they didn't talk as loud then as they do now. Maybe we all need to remember where we are; we're in a courtroom. And when we don't have the floor, we should whisper so that we don't disturb others and put ourselves in a position of being accused of coaching or acting improperly. And on this, we'd be grateful if the Defence could assist us, because if I can hear all of this chatter all the way over in this courtroom, and admittedly Courtroom I is worse than Courtroom III, but if we can hear it and if it's such a distraction to all of us over here, it's clearly within ear-shot of Defence counsel, who can understand, most of them, anyway, what the Defence are saying. And it's, in our view, their responsibility, first and foremost, to speak to their own clients and to remind their clients about how they need to be acting in the courtroom so that the Prosecution doesn't need to take the floor and to raise these issues on its own. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kruger, you have five minutes before the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, we're still dealing with Exhibit P02919, and that is the protest of Mr. Delic to Mr. Milivoj Petkovic. And -- no, it's the same document you're looking at. We're not turning to a new one. This protest by Mr. Delic to Mr. Petkovic, sir, it seems to me a continuation of the theme which we saw in the video-clip we viewed yesterday, where Mr. Halilovic asked Mr. Petkovic, Are we friends or are we enemies? Now, in the light of what we've seen previously, this morning, about Muslim residents being expelled from Mostar, East Mostar, and in the light of the one document I've shown to you which suggests a cooperative agreement between the Serbs and the Croats, are you still maintaining that the HVO has done nothing at this stage to warrant this protest by Mr. Delic?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. So when we were discussing the situation in that part of Mostar until the 30th of June, when the Croats and the Muslims were allies - that's indisputable - in Central Bosnia and Northern Herzegovina, there were clashes earlier on. But at this time when this was being written, there were large-scale conflicts in Central Bosnia, there was the BH Army attack on the HVO, and this document, in my view, it follows on from the mistakes by others. And what they failed to respect, they put the blame on to somebody else, and I've already said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, I'd like to step on to a new document. Your Honour, is there time for one more document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we have a few minutes left, and I would like to ask you a question, Witness. I would like to have the protocol that is mentioned in this document and was signed at the airport of Sarajevo on the 15th of June, 1993. And according to this document, it seems that an agreement was reached between both parties, the ABiH and the HVO, for the liberation of the prisoners -- the release of the prisoners. General Delic is not happy with the situation and gives an example. He says that, in Zenica, some captives or some prisoners -- some Croats were released, but the HVO is not stepping up to the plate, and they caught the case of the ABiH where 72 people were released, but there were 150 new prisoners. So General Delic has decided to contact General Petkovic. What I would like to know is the following: Firstly, were you aware of this agreement reached between the ABiH and the HVO on the release, as early as the 15th of June, 1993, of all prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I knew of the agreement, but all the agreement said, to release all the prisoners. But I'm certain that not all the prisoners were, in fact, released. And here only a portion in Bosnia is mentioned. There's no mention of the problems concerning Konjic. And at this particular time, when the release of prisoners is referred to, that's when the large-scale attacks were going on in Central Bosnia against the HVO units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Last question before the break. I would like to talk about the working methods of the Main Staff. This type of letter received by General Petkovic, I was wondering whether he would have a meeting with his close collaborators, such as the head of the VOS, yourself, and other people, in order to look at what is at hand and know how to answer? Were there some working meetings with everyone, or was it General Petkovic who was dealing alone with this sort of situation, or was this dealt with collectively when problems did arise?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When there were problems like this, then General Petkovic would convene the people that he thought could assist him for that particular issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I was wondering whether you took part in some meetings on various topics within the Main Staff when General Petkovic was HVO commander.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the meetings that were held, my chief, Mr. Keza, was there mostly. And as for General Petkovic, I had talks with him and contacts, let's say, since I came into service, well, just discussions at the staff, at the headquarters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question would not be complete if I did not ask the question for the period where General Praljak was in charge. I was wondering whether General Praljak had meetings with your line manager or your superior, with yourself, or with other people.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When General Praljak arrived, I was already in Sector North. And as for the meetings with the head of VOS, well, the head of VOS held regular meetings, so that was underway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. But I believe that you had already answered this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Jasak, I would like to come back to an answer you have given a bit earlier, when Mr. Antonetti confronted you with these references to prisoners. And in your answers, you said: "I'm certain that not all prisoners were, in fact, released." Now, there were prisoners taken by both sides in this, and I just wanted to know that when you said you are certain that not all prisoners were, in fact, released, whether that refers to the HVO and to the ABiH or only to one or the other.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thought that they had not been released, that is, the members of the HVO who had been held prisoner by the ABiH, which means that it wasn't true. He was still keeping the prisoners, although he said that he had released them all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: And what, then, about the allegation that the HVO had released some prisoners, but taken 150 new prisoners? Do you have any comment on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have a comment. I don't know what's correct here. However, I know, from some previous situations, that things were said at meetings to General Petkovic, that there were still prisoners who hadn't been released, and then proposals were heard to go and see where those places are, where those locations are, to prove that the HVO was right all the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, when Judge Trechsel put the question to you a moment ago, I had understood this. My question was extremely specific. I mentioned the HVO prisoners, and you answered by only discussing the HVO prisoners. I gave you the case of Kiseljak. When you answered, was it the HVO or the HVO and ABiH?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm not sure that I understood your question properly. When I answered before, what I meant was that the BiH Army had not complied with the agreement, although they say that they did. They had not complied. And in this particular time, there may have been something in Kiseljak. In any case, at that time there was an all-out attack by the BiH Army. That was a bigger problem for the HVO than the prisoners, themselves, because there was danger that the entire HVO could disappear, to be militarily defeated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, I'm logical. The letter is sent to the HVO. General Delic is questioning Mr. Petkovic about the status of the prisoners detained by the HVO. It's not the other way around. So the question only aimed at understanding what the situation for those prisoners of the HVO was. I believe you didn't understand my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether this document reflects the truth or not. Is that what you're asking me? The VOS never dealt with prisoners. However, during this specific period, when the prisoners are mentioned, that was the time of an all-out attack by the BH Army against the HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It's time to have the break. We'll have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honours, it's a small point, and it didn't affect the question and answer, but the word appears on the transcript at page 39, line 6 to 8, Judge Trechsel: "What about the allegation the HVO had released some prisoners, but taken 150 new prisoners." As it appears on the transcript, it doesn't quite accurately reflect what the document says. The document's referring to old and new prisoners. So I just thought I'd put that on the record. But I don't think it affected the answer or the way the question was understood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stewart, your objection may be upheld, since it has to do with the transcript and has nothing to do with the merits of this case, you are right to state your position.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. So far as it was an objection, I'm very happy for it to be upheld, anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: And you are absolutely right, Mr. Stewart. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you again, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We shall have a 20-minute break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session. Mr. Kruger.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, just before the break, the last document we were looking at was the protest by Mr. Delic to Mr. Petkovic, and I'd now like to -- before looking at Mr. Petkovic's response to Mr. Delic, let's have a look at some of the other things that Mr. Petkovic was doing on the same day that he responded to Mr. Delic. And for this, please turn to Exhibit P08341. It's about the fifth-last document in the binder, P08341. This exhibit is in evidence. Now, sir, this document, which is dated the 24th of June, the day after Mr. Delic's letter of protest, it's from Mr. Petkovic, Milivoj Petkovic, and it's dated 24 June 1993, and it's addressed to Rajic personally. And are you aware that this is a reference to Mr. Ivica Rajic? Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who this could be. A reference here, indeed, is to one Ivica Rajic -- to a Mr. Rajic, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, I'll just deal very quickly with this. If you look at paragraph 1, it deals with Prozor forces are working their way towards Kostajnica. Paragraph 2: "Obviously Zelic does not appreciate the situation. It will be difficult to have any effect on him." And then he says: "XY - we know he is impatient because he wants a good gift." This "XY," is this a reference, to your knowledge, to the Serbs, the Serbian side?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that this is a reference to the Serbian side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Do you know what the "good gift" reference refers to?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Right. Let's turn to the next document, then. Oh, no, sorry. Before we turn away from this document, please look at the end of the document, bullet number 5. It says: "Inundate UNPROFOR with warnings and reports." Sir, does this mean -- or you, as an analyst, would you understand this that Mr. Rajic must inundate UNPROFOR with warnings and reports about the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say that this is about the hardships of Croats in the area, and it was very difficult to get hold of UNPROFOR and inform them about the situation, if you take into account the fact that there was nothing about Croats in UNPROFOR reports, about Konjic, because UNPROFOR had not been able to enter the area, and they could only rely on the information provided to them by the Muslims. So that's how I would interpret that sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, were you aware that the HVO and the VRS were dealing with each other in MTS at this exact period in time?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that, towards the end of June, a humanitarian corridor towards Konjic was set up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Let's turn to the next exhibit, P02934. 2934. Sir, this is a document dated the 24th of June, 1993, and you'll see that it comes from Commander Ivica Rajic, and it's addressed to the head of the Defence Department and the chief of the HVO Main Staff. And it says: "Reply our query about contacts: "As regards contacts and take-over of materiel from the XY side, I have received a message that it should take place tomorrow, 25 June 1993, at 10.00, in Stolac." So, sir, "XY side," that's the Serbs, and is this, to your knowledge, a report to Mr. Stojic and Mr. Petkovic that a meeting is going to be taking place with the Serbian side in Stolac the next morning?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know, as I've already told you, that towards the end of the month, sometime after the 25th of June, contacts were established between the HVO and the VRS in connection with the evacuation of the wounded, assistance to the civilians in Turija, Zabrdje, and Zaslivlje, and opening some humanitarian corridors for the benefit of those people. And I know that it happened sometime around that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, this is for the take-over of materiel from the XY side. Is it correct that the HVO was dealing with these Serbs behind the backs of their allies, the Muslims, at this time?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what materiel is referred to here, but I know that that time, possibly on the 25th of June, General Petkovic was supposed to meet with Grubac and to agree to details of assistance to be provided to people in the territory of Konjic; how to look after them, how to treat them, how to supply them with food, how to assist the civilians, including the sick and the wounded. The humanitarian disaster in the territory of Konjic was out of any proportion, and I know that something was done in order to deal with that situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Let's turn -- sir, at this stage, this is six days before the attack of the 30th of June, and you confirm that the HVO and the ABiH are still --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, regarding this document, if we look at all the documents shown to us by the Prosecution, I don't know exactly what this is all about. This is materiel, equipment, money. I don't know. Maybe this has to do with materiel, equipment. I just have some small idea. I see that Rajic's response is also addressed to the Defence Department. So, as you can see, there are two addressees here, Defence Department and HVO Main Staff. The Defence Department was involved with logistical matters. This may have had to do with equipment or materiel, which means that it would have been of concern to the Defence Department, which would explain why the Defence Department was one of the addressees of Rajic's response to General Petkovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there's not much text in here. It doesn't lend itself to a very good understanding. However, judging by the date, I know that sometime around that time Generals Petkovic and Grubac met in order to agree the details of the humanitarian corridor and the assistance to the area, in terms of food, medicines, clothes. For months, nothing had reached those people who had been completely isolated for months. I'm talking about Turija, Zabrdje, and Zaslivlje, as parts of Konjic municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, let's quickly, just to see what we're really talking about, turn to Exhibit P02966. It's about five or six documents further on from where you are. P02966. This a document dated 26 June 1993, and again it's from Ivica Rajic, and it's addressed to the chief of the Main Staff and the head of the Defence Department. It says: "Update on co-operation with XY side: "As per your advice and as per their request of yesterday, earlier this morning I sent a request to the main person on the XY side. Around 3.00, I received a message that my request was on Ratko's desk and that they could deliver 30 rifles immediately at 5.000 Deutschmarks each." Sir, the materiel we're talking about is weapons. There was weapons transactions going -- arms transactions going on between the HVO and the Serbs at that time; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to read the entire document to see what it's about, but I said that a humanitarian corridor was being opened during that time and that assistance was being provided to the civilian population in the territories of Turija, Zabrdje, and Zaslivlje.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, sir, let's look at the response of General Petkovic to Mr. Delic on the 24th of June, 1993. It's Exhibit P02938, and it's about four documents before. P02938. It's by General Petkovic, and it's addressed -- and it's "Reply to Protest of the 4th Corps." And it says: "Your protest is insincere, unobjective, and self-incriminating." Sir, I put it to you, and I want your reaction, isn't it so that actually, from what we've seen, General Petkovic is the one who's not being honest here?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, an objection with regard to the presentation of the document. The document doesn't have anything whatsoever to do with the prior -- Rasim Delic's letter. This is just an answer to a protest from the 4th Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kruger, you have shown us a letter of protest. After that, you showed a document mentioning XY. Now you are showing us Mr. Petkovic's response. I also find it difficult to follow, the logic. We can hear the witness's answer, but I feel a little bit like Ms. Alaburic does. I don't quite understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll rephrase the question and put it not in the context, then, of Mr. Delic's letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, in this letter of the 24th of June, a reply to a protest of the 4th Corps, do you see any reference there that the HVO is dealing with the common enemy, the Serbs, regarding weapons?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you can see here is that this is an answer to a protest from the 4th Corps. I don't know what protest was that. It was sent to the 4th Corps, to UNPROFOR in Medjugorje, and UNPROFOR in Kiseljak. I'm sure that the document would not have been sent to all those addresses if it was to be kept secret. It says: "Your protest is insincere," and this is an answer to the commander of the 4th Corps, which means that everybody knew what the situation in Mostar was like, and everybody is warned to adhere to the terms of the cease-fire. And this we already mentioned with regard to (redacted). I've already spoken about that at great length. There was some renegade groups that roamed around the city, and that was prevented -- or at least attempts were made to prevent that by introducing joint patrols and a curfew. All that was done to prevent them from creating havoc around town and shooting. It says here: "On our part, we are exerting influence and shall continue doing so to ensure that the cease-fire is observed." And I'm telling you that this protest is just a cover-up for the plans to fuel up the conflict in Mostar. Every time they said something to that effect and accused the HVO, it was always done to lay the ground for some future offensive activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, please turn to the next document in the binder, which is P02946. This document is already in evidence, P02946. No, my apologies, Your Honour, it's not in evidence yet. That's my mistake. I misspoke. Sir, this is a BritBat report coming from the -- or dated the 25th of June, 1993, and it says, paragraph 1: "Indigenous forces: "A. OP Grapple: "1. Bosnian Serb leader Radovan Karadzic said today that he and Bosnian Croat leader Mate Boban had agreed on the creation of a confederation of three ethnic mini-states in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and called on Bosnia's Muslims to come to the negotiating table." Did you know about such an agreement taking place around the 25th of June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And if such a mini-state were agreed, would you disagree that the Croatian ethnic mini-state would be the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna's area?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no knowledge of them talking or having agreed on something. As far as I know, Croats negotiated only under the auspices of the international community. I'm not aware of any such conversations having taken place ever.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you, as an analyst, appealing to your skills as an analyst now, seeing this, would you agree that this agreement between the Serbs and the Croats, without the Muslims being present, threatens the existence of the RBiH?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what the meaning of the mini-state is in this context. All three sides are being requested to negotiate. I don't know what about. I suppose there could not have been any negotiations without the international community, so nobody would be at a risk. Three sides are mentioned in here, and they're urged to sit at a negotiating table. What is meant by that, I don't know. I've already told you that I don't know. But I know that whenever the Croats sat down to negotiate anything, for example, the future organisation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, they did it exclusively under the auspices of the international community.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, let's turn to two documents further on, then, P02953. And this document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before moving on to the next document, I would like to look at this internal document of the British Army. This is not an UNPROFOR document. Unless I'm mistaken, this is a document which comes from the British Army. Therefore, this is an internal document which does not engage the international community at large; only the British Army. Let's look at the first page, the beginning of the first page, the top, paragraph A, paragraph 3. It says the BritBat reports states that there has been an ABiH offensive in the Bila Valley, but that this offensive is seemingly suspended for a while due to the fact that there is an issue with the Serbs along the front-line. This document is dated in the month of June. This document comes from the British Army. This seems to indicate that the ABiH is attacking in the Bila Valley, at any rate. Does this coincide with what you knew?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question was a bit too long. I know that the BH Army at the time did engage in attacks in the area against the HVO. I know that for a fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have seen how this report was translated in your language. Does this confirm that it was the ABiH that was attacking in this valley?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The BiH Army did launch attacks in the valley.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Could you also say attacks against whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The BiH Army launched attacks against the HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, if we can turn to document P02953. Okay. Sir, this is a document from Commander Marinko Puljic, and it's dated "Stolac, 25 June 1993," a daily report. And about two sentences or a few lines down, it says: "At 10.30, the military police increased road security due to the arrival of General Petkovic, who was on his way to negotiate with the Serbs. "Negotiations lasted until 1.00, when Petkovic returned." I ask you again. Were you aware that General Petkovic was negotiating with the Serbs at this time?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: To follow up on the previous documents, those were negotiations towards establishing a humanitarian corridor in Turija, Zabrdje, and Zaslivlje, and towards assisting those people who had been inaccessible for months. If we're talking about the 25th of June, it was on that day. I know that it happened sometime after the 24th. So that would be that, definitely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Have a look at the very next document, sir, P02962. This is a document -- communication from General Petkovic to Mr. Rajic, and it says: "Inform the other side that we completely accept the already-concluded agreement on MTS on their conditions. We will carry out the duty you have outlined." Paragraph 2: "At the last meeting in Sarajevo, two commanders discussed the possibility of help, and Mr. Stojic was given assurances by the other side's two main political leaders that there would be no problems during the delivery of MTS." And then look at point 5: "Also request artillery support, and explain that helping us also means helping them." Sir, does this not indicate that General Petkovic is asking the common enemy of the HVO and -- or suggesting that the common enemy of the HVO and the ABiH should be shelling or helping in shelling the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already told you that I have no knowledge of any such activities, except the matter linked to Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, all these documents that I have shown you, these past few documents, are all dated a few days before the 30th of June, 1993, when that Muslim attack occurred. Now, I put it to you that at this stage, for any analyst on the other side it would have been clear that the ABiH's ally, the HVO, had turned against them and had linked up to fight against them with the Serbs. Isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not so, and for this reason: As far as Mostar is concerned, the very day before the 30th the joint forces -- our joint forces held the line in the area from Bijelo Polje southwards -- south of Mostar, so those are the facts. And it is my assumption here that this was linked to Konjic, because it was a very, very difficult situation there at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And, sir, I put it to you that for the Muslim members within the HVO at that stage, all these indications that I've shown you would have made them very concerned about the sincerity of the HVO, because they were in the HVO to fight against the Serbs, yet it seemed that the HVO commanders or leadership had actually become friends with the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honours, objection, because it is presumed that the Muslim soldiers within the HVO knew something about co-operation with the Serb side, and the objection is based on the following: Whether it refers to Muslims in the Mostar HVO brigades, and, if so, how could they know what was happening, for example, in the area of Central Bosnia or in the Turija-Zabrdje-Zaslivlje enclave?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may very briefly respond. The documents that I've shown have not only referred to what Ms. Alaburic has referred to. We've also shown the witness evidence or information showing that Muslims were being expelled from Mostar, we've shown information regarding co-operation with the Serbs regarding MTS, and reports -- internal HVO reports going around. So certainly there was every chance that soldiers on the ground may also have picked up these goings on, and I'm simply asking the witness whether he is able to comment on this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you mentioned expulsions, the Muslims -- well, had it been the way it says in this report, well, the Muslims would have left the HVO far earlier, would they not, because at the time a large number of Muslims were in the HVO and on the right bank of the Neretva River. So especially this bit here, this refers to a completely different area that had nothing to do with Mostar, and it was a humanitarian issue. Here, the talks and negotiations between the HVO and the Army of Republika Srpska, as far as I know, referred to Konjic and the humanitarian corridor during that period of time. That's when this was discussed. And General Petkovic and the command on the Serb side discussed the issue, and attempts were always made to calm the situation down. And Mostar was the last town where this kind of conflict took place, so this couldn't affect the people.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter notes: On the Serb side, it was General Grubac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a second. I have been listening to your comments regarding humanitarian issues, and if I understand you correctly, you needed to have an agreement with the Serbs and to give them some MTS, and in exchange you could solve the humanitarian problems. Why not? However, paragraph 5 is talking about the artillery, and what does it have to do with this in the picture? Why are we asking the artillery support? What has artillery got to do in such a dispensation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the people who were in the enclave did not have any artillery, so that's what that is about. If they were to be attacked, to defend them. I don't know what else it could mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, in the few minutes remaining, I'd like to turn to my final topic, and I'd like to turn -- or explore your assertion that the HVO -- in the HVO at the time, there was no real opportunity to exercise effective command. And this is what you said on the 18th of January, transcript reference T-48491 at line 15, and you were responding to a document shown to you regarding HVO soldiers protesting salaries in 1994. On the basis of that, you said there was no real opportunity to exercise effective control, or "effective command" were your exact words. Sir, from that, are we to understand that no single order that was ever issued by any officer in the HVO was obeyed?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never said anything like that, that no order was ever obeyed. But as for meetings of this kind, I said I knew that they were held.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: So you would agree, then, that combat orders were entirely possible and could be obeyed; it wasn't necessary, when you were being attacked or when you wanted to launch an attack, to first negotiate with your troops? A commander could issue an order, and it would be obeyed; that was entirely possible?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I knew of only one attack operation by the HVO against the Army of Republika Srpska in 1992 and what the problems were. So the problem was to persuade people to come up to the front-line, let alone some offensive operations, so I don't know what this is about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, from what you've just said, you're not saying that it wasn't at all possible -- or, rather, from what you said, it is possible orders could be issued by commanders to their troops for combat operations, which would be obeyed? It was possible in the HVO? A simple yes or no.

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That wasn't the question. The question was, Is it possible to issue orders? Now, whether they were carried out, that's another question, but there was no offensive action at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, in a further part of your evidence you made the point, and your exact words were: "The HVO was a defensive army exclusively." Do you stand by that?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, the HVO was a defensive army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: All right. Let's turn to Exhibit P06534, P06534. It's an exhibit which is already in evidence. Now, sir, this is an order from General Petkovic, dated the 8th of November, 1993, and it's titled "Order for Offensive Combat Operations." And it's addressed to various addressees, and it says: "In order to defend these Croatian territories, I hereby order: "The HVO units on all sectors of the front must switch to offensive operations immediately." Sir, do you agree that from this it appears there are two distinct modes, one of defence and one of offence, two modes?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a document which came into being when I wasn't in the staff, at the headquarters. But, on the other hand, I can try and interpret this as an order as it stands. It means that when active defence is engaged in, it has a certain -- in a certain segment, it is offensive.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you, but the question is simply -- and a yes or no would suffice. Is it clear from this there would be two modes, defence and offence, switch from the one mode to the other in this regard?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'd just like the witness to allow -- to respond to the question asked. And if you look at the introduction to this order, regardless of who the author of the order is, it will be precisely what the witness started to say. And I think that it is in the Judges' interest to hear what the witness wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, what did you want to say, exactly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll try, Your Honours. The fall, so this is one period when Vares fell, and there were a large number of refugees in that period. Now, the Muslim forces continued their offensive operations in the area of the Lasva River Valley and the Zepa region, so throughout this area of Central Bosnia, the aim was to route the HVO militarily. Now, to defend the Croatian areas, an order is issued to the effect that the HVO units must switch to offensive operations. It says "offensive operations," and that is support and reinforcement to active defence, which means to lift the burden of the small area that had not been routed by the BH Army. But you cannot imply that they launched offensive operations, the attack. So the units that you have primarily intended there for defence, the efforts made were to try and help these units and to prevent the total defeat of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Kruger.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Witness, it sounds to me like you're playing semantics, because certainly to just call an operation defensive, it doesn't change the fact that if you order an attack, you can order an attack. It was possible in the HVO, and they were doing it; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was very concrete here, and I know that it was about a large number of displaced persons and refugees from the area. So we can see that Vares had fallen, and we also see that there were attacks against the Lasva River Valley in its entirety, and the Zepa area. And then, with what forces you had available, they tried to save what could be saved, catch as catch can. So there were no attack operations to gain control of territory, but to save what could be salvaged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kruger, there might be an issue with words here. It might not be only a question of semantics or playing with words. From a military point of view, you were in the military - I don't know whether Mr. Kruger ever was - but you are a colonel at the moment and I assume that you must have looked at military history. Perhaps you looked at what had happened during the Second World War. Perhaps you were aware of the Von Rundstedt offensive in 1994 and 1995 [as interpreted] in the Belgian Ardennes and in Luxembourg. This was an offensive operation, and perhaps you were aware of the counter-attack or counter-offensive of the allied armies against this German general. So in military terms, you have an offensive and then you have a counter-offensive or counter-attack. In the document, the ABiH had an operation in Vares. That's what the document says. And then the HVO is defending itself. It says "in order to defend" in the document. So I was wondering whether the relevant military term should have been an order for counter-offensive.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Vares had already fallen here, by this time, and we know what happened when Vares fell, what the problems were. And what is sought here is, if you look at the area, to lift the burden and to have the Novi Travnik-Gornji Vakuf access to help them, and the Kiseljak-Busovaca access. So we know that Kiseljak had been cut off from Busovaca. We know that everything was under siege up there, and it was a very difficult situation. So what is stated here, exactly, is less important. What is essential is that the primary thing was to defend the area and to send reinforcements and help, because in the last point -- or, rather, point 4, the Vitez Military District, with all available forces, put up a persistent and decisive defence. That's what it says in point 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I was wondering whether, in your language, there is such a term as "counter-offensive."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it does. "Counter-offensive," "counter-attack."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. And so why is this term not used in the document, and do you think it should have been used? If you don't know, you can just say so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think this here, too, is visible; that is to say, you could use that. But from this, we can see what the goal and intention was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed, Mr. Kruger.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Mr. Jasak, I only wish to show you three more documents on this topic, and that's all I'll have time for. Please turn to P00460. I think it should be about the first document in the binder. P00460. Now, this is an order by Colonel Siljeg to the Eugen Kvaternik Brigade to assist the possibility of elimination of Muslim forces in Gornji Vakuf, and it's dated the 27th of October, 1992. And if you look after the -- two paragraphs above his -- sorry. If you look below the title, it says: "We immediately request information on the situation in ..." various areas, and then he says: "Provide estimate of a possibility of passage on the roads," and he mentions the route, and then he says: "Provide an estimate of a possibility of eliminating the Muslim forces in Gornji Vakuf." Now, sir, that sounds to me like offensive language. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see anything here that smacks of offensive.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, you're an analyst.

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: A report is called for here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: But certainly, sir, as an analyst, you would appreciate that to eliminate the Muslim forces in Gornji Vakuf would require a positive action on the side of the HVO. They would need to attack those forces in order -- before they could eliminate them. So doesn't this show that in the thinking of the HVO, certainly it did see itself as capable of attack as well; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not. Here it says "assess the possibilities," but we should take into account what this is all about in the first place. So during that period in Vakuf, trenches were being dug facing Croatian villages, not facing the Army of Republika Srpska. And what is called for here is a possibility, an assessment, an appraisal; nothing specific, nothing concrete.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, just before stepping off this: On the last part of the document, to the second paragraph above Mr. Siljeg's signature, or Mr. Siljeg's name, at least, it says -- it's the paragraph starting: "We are expecting a Merhamet convoy," and it goes on: "... check whether they have permission for transporting weapons issued by the Minister of Defence, Gojko Susak, or General Praljak; in case they don't have these ..." Is it correct that General Mr. Praljak at that stage was also involved in the whole process of arms transport to the HVO?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to read this first, because you've said your bit and now I have to read it to see what it's about, because it's a document of the 9th of September, 1992. And, at the time, I was commander in Mostar, of the battalion in Mostar. So I want to see what this is all about and what this is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kruger, I was wondering whether this document would not be the compilation of two documents, actually. If you look at the B/C/S version, I have the feeling that they were two documents that were put together in one, they were copied. And the English translations lead us to believe that there's only one document that was signed by Siljeg, whereas, in fact, in the B/C/S version we are dealing with two documents. There is a document, and you're right in saying, that has got to do with the assessment of the situation in Gornji Vakuf, and then you have a second document which has to do with humanitarian convoys. Am I mistaken?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, no, you're entirely correct. And in trying to finish, it slipped my attention now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: So indeed, Mr. Jasak, the document you're looking at now is a second document, and it's dated the 9th of September, 1992. The question, however, stands. In September 1992, was General Praljak involved in the process of providing arms to the HVO or other forces?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We can see here that this was about supplying ABiH Army with weapons. Those were Muslims forces, and the supplier was Merhamet, which was their own organisation. Now, what was the case at the time? I said I don't know. This was probably assistance that arrived from Croatia to the Muslim forces through their humanitarian organisation Merhamet, which is very similar to what Caritas was for the Catholic population.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, let's look at the second-last document, P01107. It's the fourth document in the binder, P01107.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Kruger. I'm sorry to interrupt you, but I have to come back to this document, because, in his answer, Mr. Jasak mentioned, and I quote, that: "We can see here this was about supplying ABiH Army with weapons. Those were Muslim forces, and the supplier was Merhamet, which is the organisation. Now, what was the case at the time? I said I don't know. ... the Muslim forces, through their humanitarian organisation Merhamet, which is very similar to what Caritas was for the Catholic population." Now, I believe that, of course, we have to speak about two issues distinctly. One thing is Merhamet, but here, in this particular order, there is a reference that, and I quote here from it: "... check whether they have permission for transporting weapons issued by the Minister of Defence, Gojko Susak, or General Praljak; in case they don't have these authorisations, unload them and inform the zone command." So I believe that this particular part is addressing a question not about Merhamet, not about humanitarian assistance, but about transporting weapons. And then I ask the witness if he knew about those issues and if -- according to his reading and according to his knowledge, if some permission for transporting weapons were issued by the Croatian Minister of Defence Gojko Susak or at that time, in 1992, by General Praljak. It is the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'll try and clarify a bit. I said that during that period, I was involved in certain matters, but I knew what Merhamet is. It's a humanitarian Muslim organisation. I know that at the time assistance was extended by the Republic of Croatia both to the HVO and the BiH Army. The Republic of Croatia armed everybody who fought against the VRS. I suppose that some people had spoken with Siljeg, told him that they had been provided with that from Mr. Praljak or Mr. Susak, and they probably wanted to check whether that was indeed the case. I don't know what else could be at stake, because I was not involved in the work of higher commands. All I know is that the arming of the BiH Army and the HVO was done through almost identical channels and almost in an identical way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, let's turn to Exhibit P01107. It's the fourth document in your binder, and this is an order from Colonel Siljeg on the 12th of January, 1993, and it's in regard to the action of the Operational Zone of North-West Herzegovina, forces in Gornji Vakuf and Bugojno, and it's to all operational zone brigades. And he says -- he orders, number 1: "The attack forces of the operational zone and other forces from Ante Starcevic, Eugen Kvaternik, and Rama Brigades are to route the enemy forces in Bugojno and Gornji Vakuf with the following objective: "Take control of towns and roads." Number 2, if we continue: "A. The Rama Brigade is to block the Jablanica-Prozor road and secure our force's right flank." The next sentence: "Its main forces, co-operating with the forces of the Ante Starcevic Brigade, are to route the enemy at Karamustapic's area." And then if we go to B, it says: "The main force of the Ante Starcevic Brigade are to engage and clear the BH Army forces in Gornji Vakuf, secure the Gornji Vakuf." And then it says a bit further on: "Ensure that the Rama Brigade can launch an offensive, crush the enemy in the Osredak-Voljice area, and prevent the BH Army forces from intervening from the direction of Rostovo." "C: Crush the enemy forces in Bugojno once again." And my question to you, sir, is clearly: The HVO has an attack capability; it is not purely a defensive army, as you alleged?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
