utterances.text: The HVO did not have the capacity for attack, and one has to see what was the effect of that. So it wasn't as it says here; it was not the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: So this order, as it stands on the paper, there's not interpretation? This is not an attack order, according to you, to the HVO brigades in this operational zone; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, we're talking about an area which was not under the South-Eastern Herzegovina Operational Zone. I'm trying to see what is in the area of responsibility that was my primary responsibility. I would have to go back and try to remind myself of what was going on on the 12th of January, what was happening, what was topical in the area. I would have to read this at a bit greater length and see what the reasons might have been for anything to be launched. To be talking on top of my head is impossible. I would have to see the details of the situation. I know that there were no offensive activities going on. Everything was done to support defence or what I mentioned under the term "active defence," in order to bring the defence in a favourable situation, not to take control of anything. So when you are defending yourself, you do engage in some activities that do feature elements of attack, but they're still defence activities, not offence activities. We're not talking about reaching certain lines in order to launch a defence activity. This is just support to the defence activities for the troops to reach a more favourable position.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, a correction for the record. In the second sentence of the answer, the witness is recorded as saying, "This was my primary responsibility," and what he said was that he was trying to discern what was happening in the area that was not his primary responsibility, because Gornji Vakuf belonged to the area of North-West Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says here : "Due to the deterioration of the situation between Croats and Muslims and the BiH Army attempting to take some vital facilities in Gornji Vakuf," which are under the control of the HVO. We're talking about some vital positions where the HVO already had its troops deployed, and the BH Army was attempting to take them. That's what is written in the first sentence. Constant incidents, removing the Croatian flag from its position in the center of town, the arrest of people, and the arrival of the troops of the BiH Army from Central Bosnia, rather than locals in Gornji Vakuf; the non-functioning of civilian authorities, and especially in view of the attempts to eliminate the HVO in Gornji Vakuf on the part of the BiH Army. During that period, I know that that was sometime in January, joint commissions were set up with the task of calming the situation down, so this is a consequence of the activities of the BiH Army. And attempts were made to alleviate the situation by way of launching an active defence. This is a reaction, and you can see what the reaction is to. And we said already that there were trenches dug out facing the HVO and not the VRS. There was a problem here of the Muslims who had been expelled by the Serbs from Donji Vakuf who found themselves in that area, which caused many incidents. You can see that there was also a problem of the flag. Only the Muslim flag was allowed to be hoisted and not a Croatian flag.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, let's turn to the final document I'm going to show you. It's the very next document in your binder. It's P -- no, it's about two on, I think. P01162 is the next document, P01162. Now, sir, this is a regular report by Colonel Zeljko Siljeg, and it's dated the 16th of January, 1993. And if I can remind you, we've spoken about this earlier. The Prosecution's position is that this is at the time that an ultimatum was directed by the HVO to the ABiH in January 1993 to submit themselves. Now, in this regular report, which reports on negotiations between the HVO and the ABiH in Gornji Vakuf, turn to the second-last paragraph, please. And it says: "Tonight at Gornji Vakuf, Colonel Siljeg and Colonel Andric negotiated with BH Army representatives. There were no results. Unless there is an agreement, Gornji Vakuf, southern strongholds, will be taken and our line strengthened." And then General Praljak sent them a message that they will be annihilated if they do not accept the decisions of the HZ-HB. Now, sir, my first question to you is that in order to annihilate the ABiH, that would require an attack from the HVO; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: An attack would have been necessary. But I repeat, this is an area which was not my primary concern. I would have to read the entire order or, rather, the entire report. When I see a reference to Colonel Andric, I know that he was trying to calm the situation down in Bugojno, Vakuf, Prozor, as I've already said. As for the dates referred to herein, and when you look at the word "step over," this is a colloquialism. I don't know what that would mean, but I know that at the time there were no strong offence activities. I know that at the time, in the area of this territory, we had suffered losses. We had fallen men who would be found by the road, massacred, and in every shape and form. The situation was rife with incidents on the ground. How they developed, I don't know. And how the conversations and talks went on, I really can't tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, the final part, which says General Praljak sent them a message: "They will be annihilated if they do not accept the decisions of the HZ-HB, the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna." Doesn't this reflect the entire attitude of the HVO during 1992 and 1993, being only the will of the HVO matters, Whatever the ABiH says or decides is totally irrelevant; it's our will, and we will enforce our will? Wasn't that the situation?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The situation was absolutely not the way you describe it. I know that towards the end of 1992 and the beginning of 1993, Colonel Andric and General Praljak arrived in the area and helped dig up the trenches. They didn't want to dig up the trenches that were facing Croatian villages, and somehow they managed to agree with the local commanders as to how to organise lines facing the Chetniks and link up all the local commanders. The HVO did everything in its ability to calm the situation down, but somebody added fuel to the fire, obviously. And this is just one sentence. What was the context? I don't know. But I'm sure that this was not an official position or a rule of behaviour. When you look at the dates, then you know that positions were being reinforced facing the VRS, alleviate tension in the town of Gornji Vakuf, Bugojno, and Prozor, and to engage joint forces in order to defend those areas.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your permission, I would like to react to the record. I suppose that my colleague Suzanna wanted to do the same thing. On line 13 of the record I'm looking at now, it says that the witness alleged that they didn't want to dig up the trenches. The witness actually said they didn't want to fill up the trenches. "Fill up" was the words the witness used.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And maybe just one thing about the same period and one more mistake in the transcript with regard to the digging or filling of trenches. On page 68 -- I've lost it now. Page 68, line 16, the witness said that General Praljak arrived and helped to fill the trenches up, whereas in the record it says that he helped dig trenches. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And maybe one more thing to be said about the same period. In the VOS, we had intelligence that the VRS -- we intercepted that information. The VRS said, Pound once and then pound the others. They added a bit more fuel to the situation. And that's how things were done. They pounded once and then they pounded the others in the area, until the moment Operation Maslenica was launched in Croatia. And that's when they had to dispatch some of their troops to go to that area and engage in that offensive.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And, sir, my final question to you, and the point may have been lost due to the corrections in the transcript. The point -- the question that I'd asked you is -- from what we see General Praljak said, the question is: Doesn't this reflect the entire attitude of the HVO, that only the will of the HVO mattered, whatever the ABiH did was irrelevant? Now, you've given your response to that, and now my final question to you is, sir: I've been listening to you for seven days now, and despite many documents being shown to you which suggest that the HVO does not entirely have clean hands, you were not once able to find any criticism regarding the actions of the HVO, and isn't it so, sir, that in your eyes the HVO could do no wrong?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the HVO is concerned, I was talking from the point of view of the Main Staff about some general positions. There were some incidents on the ground. However, at the Main Staff level, initiatives were launched to always calm the situation down. And in this case, the situation was the same. I believe that Colonel Andric, Miro Andric, was sent as an experienced person, a person who knew a lot about the Muslims. He hailed from Konjic. That's where he was born. He was brought up and raised in Bijelo Polje, near Mostar. He was in command of the 1st Bijelo Polje Battalion, where 50 per cent of the men were Muslims, and he was a successful commander. For a while, he was also the deputy chief of the Main Staff. And if a person of that kind is given a mission to calm the situation down, and if a person of that kind is sent to an area, the intention is clear, the agenda is clear. A maximum is being invested to calm the situation down and to try and engage joint forces in a battle against a common enemy. As far as Central Bosnia is concerned, as well as North-West Herzegovina and the area of responsibility there, the majority of the population there were Muslims, and most troops were Muslims. They prevailed, and launching any military activity there was not logical from a military point of view. The only thing that could be done was to reach an agreement and act jointly against a common enemy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jasak. No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Kruger. We shall have a 20-minute break now and resume with the redirect afterwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Court is back in session. Judge Prandler has a medical appointment, and therefore he cannot be with us from now on. We're going to move to redirect. Ms. Alaburic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Jasak, let's try and clarify certain details . First of all, tell us which body in Herceg-Bosna had at its disposal the most complete information about the enemy armies, or the enemy army, as a singular, depending on the time-frame.

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the VOS of the Main Staff of the HVO, the VOS standing for the Military Intelligence Service.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALABURIC
utterances.text: When it comes to the VOS, which person had the most complete information about the enemy armies, or the enemy army, singular, in the territory of the South-East Herzegovina OZ?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was the one who had the most complete information, together with the chief for whom I prepared reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If I understood you properly, with all of your colleagues you worked in one room, you shared one room, and your chief had a separate office. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALABURIC
utterances.text: When it comes to your colleagues, if they monitored the situation in Central Bosnia, would they inform you about any issues relevant for the understanding of the situation in the South-East Herzegovina OZ?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, they would. We discussed those matters, and I reciprocated with the information coming from the South-East Herzegovina OZ.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did the VOS receive intelligence from the territory about crimes that may have been committed by an HVO member or any other illegal actions performed by any of the troops?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not receive such information or intelligence because we were not authorised to receive such information.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness's answer either be interpreted or -- I apologise. My mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jasak, I'm now going to follow the sequence of the Prosecutor's cross-examination in chief, which is the simplest way for me to go about things. Let's first look at the document in the Prosecutor's binder, 6534. You can see it on the screen in front of you. Your Honours, all the documents that I was able to prepare yesterday are to be found in a binder, and they follow a certain sequence, but I'm also going to be referring to some documents that have been used by the Prosecutor today and we did not have the time to include them in the binder. One of the last orders that the Prosecutor showed you was the order dated 8 November 1993, in which bears the name of Milivoj Petkovic. At the moment, we are not going to dwell upon who the author of the order actually was. To follow up on His Honour Judge Antonetti's questions, Judge Antonetti asked you whether we have the term "counter-offensive" in our language, and you said that, Yes, we do have that term in our language. Mr. Jasak, if we take Vares, for example, which was taken by the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, what would be a counter-offensive with regard to the situation of the fall of Vares?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would start with the grouping of forces and the return to Vares, which means that Vares would have to be re-taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If I understand you properly, a counter-offensive would be an attack launched in order to return control over the territory that had been lost. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now let's look at this order. Does this order relate to a counter-offensive against Vares or any other part of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not an order for counter-offensive against Vares or any other part of Bosnia and Herzegovina. We can see that an order is issued to the effect that I have already explained, to alleviate the burden of the remaining forces on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In the introductory part of this order, it says: "In order to defend the aforementioned Croatian areas," namely, the Lasva Valley and the area of Zepa?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, the Lasva Valley and the area of Zepa which came under threat. The forces that launched attacks against Lasva Valley and the area of Zepa had to be redirected, and that's why all the activities were undertaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The two areas in question, are they Croatian enclaves in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, those were two Croatian enclaves in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALABURIC
utterances.text: A different topic now. The Prosecutor asked you about a document issued by the British Battalion. The number of the document -- and you just listen to me. The number is P2946. It is in the Prosecutor's binder of documents. It is dated 25th June 1993. It is actually a report of Radovan Karadzic having said that he had met with Boban and agreed for Bosnia and Herzegovina to exist as a co-confederation of three national mini-states. Do you remember that document, Mr. Jasak?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember it, and I can see it on the screen at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, did you ever hear about the Owen-Stoltenberg Plan?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Some unions of republics are also referred to in that plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And that plan, was that for Bosnia and Herzegovina to be a union of three republics?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that that was the gist of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, did that plan become topical in mid-1993?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It became topical after the Serbs had turned down the Vance-Owen Plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALABURIC
utterances.text: When did the Serbs turn down the Vance-Owen Plan?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: They turned it down -- they rejected it sometime after the meeting in Athens. I believe that it was in June 1993. There was a referendum to that effect. Karadzic had even signed it, but it was nevertheless rejected after the referendum, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes, you're absolutely right, sir. The Vance-Owen Plan that my learned friend Mr. Kruger asked you about, when did Croats sign the Vance-Owen Plan?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in January 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did that plan envisage for Bosnia and Herzegovina to be a state composed of 10 provinces?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And if those provinces had been established, would that mean that Herceg-Bosna would disappear?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. There would no longer be a need for Herceg-Bosna because the state would have been otherwise organised.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And now, Mr. Jasak, explain one thing, please. The leadership of Herceg-Bosna in January 1993, was it aware of the fact that if provinces were organised in Bosnia-Herzegovina, that would mean that Herceg-Bosna would disappear?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, there was no reason for them not to be aware of that. It was very clear, because it was well known that Herceg-Bosna was a temporary body that was meant to be put in place to organise the defence of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I apologise to my learned colleague to interrupt. I do not want to disrupt her re-examination. I would just request that she be careful with regard to leading questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am really trying hard, and I believe that my question was not leading. My question lent itself to all sorts of different answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, if provinces had been established in Bosnia and Herzegovina, Herceg-Bosna would disappear; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Herceg-Bosna would have disappeared and would have been replaced by the provinces, and what would have remained was Bosnia and Herzegovina, as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did the Croatian side in Bosnia and Herzegovina, according to what you know, do anything in order to prevent the implementation of the Vance-Owen Peace Plan?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, the Croatian side did not do anything to that effect. They did not do anything to prevent the implementation of the plan, and that is why the Croatian side accepted the plan as the first signatory of it, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor suggested to you or put it to you that the Muslim side in Bosnia and Herzegovina was against, and I quote, "the idea of Herceg-Bosna." Mr. Jasak, could you explain to us how come that the Muslim side did not accept, or at least not immediately, an organisation of Bosnia-Herzegovina that would involve the disappearance of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: My only explanation would be that there were some people who wanted exclusively a unitarian Bosnia-Herzegovina without any provinces. I don't know what else could have been the reason. There were some forces in action that wanted Bosnia and Herzegovina to be created as a state of just one people or one nation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALABURIC
utterances.text: What about your personal view about the unitarian -- about a unitarian Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would have been a state that would uphold the interests of only one people, and the others would not have had any rights. There would have been just one person, one vote, and in such a state, other peoples would not have been able to defend any of their interests; if they were minorities, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that you knew a lot of Croats, would you say that they shared your views of the unitarian Bosnia-Herzegovina or was there a difference between yourself and the others? I'm talking about your acquaintances and friends.

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: My acquaintances and friends shared my view.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I am again trying to elicit your personal position. At the time when you were a member of the HVO, did there come a time when you started thinking that you were doing something that would not have been appropriate for the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina and that probably led to the separation of some parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never thought that I was working towards that goal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jasak, let's move on to a different topic. The Prosecutor asked you about the Muslim Army and the HVO, whether they were allies between the 9th of May, 1993, to the 30th of June, 1993, and you said that they were, indeed. Could you please tell us, which area did your answer refer to?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer referred to the area of Mostar, because those two dates were very important in terms of the city of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And the Prosecutor showed you a number of documents to contradict your answer, and showed that in certain areas the HVO and the VRS co-operated. If we sum up those documents and if we tally them with your answer, we will see that those documents referred to the area of Kiseljak and the supply of humanitarian aid through the Croatian enclaves near Konjic, Turija, Zabrdje, and Zaslivlje. My question, sir: The areas of Kiseljak and Kresevo, were those areas Croatian enclaves?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And did that enclave lean, in part, on a territory which was under Serb control?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALABURIC
utterances.text: To the best of your knowledge, under such conditions, that is to say, in an encirclement, was the possibility of collaborating with the Serbs a prerequisite for the survival of the Croats in that enclave?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, any kind of co-operation, well, it meant pure survival. I was speaking about Konjic, mostly, because that was in my primary zone of activity, which is something I knew about, and I also knew that that co-operation was realised only when a humanitarian catastrophe was looming.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, Witness, the Croatian enclaves in the Konjic area in May and June, how many enclaves were there?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was one enclave, Turija-Zabrdje-Zaslivlje. That was one. Then there was another one around the Neretvica.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALABURIC
utterances.text: When you say in the area of the Neretvica, does that mean around the town of Kostajnica?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's actually a village, not a town.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Right, village. This other enclave around Kostajnica, did it lean, in part, on territory controlled by the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And did the enclave exist at the end of July 1993?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it disappeared by then.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The other enclave by Konjic, Turija-Zabrdje-Zaslivlje, did it lean, in part of its territory, on the territory under Serb control?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And did that enclave survive to the end of the conflict with the Muslim Army?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, since it's your area, do you have any knowledge whether the possibility of co-operating with the Serbs and collaborating with them had an influence on the survival of that enclave?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only by collaborating with the Serbs was it possible to survive, for the enclave to survive, because before this collaboration with the Serbs, there were humanitarian attempts, attempts via international organisations. Various pressure was brought to bear, sending letters stating that the situation was catastrophic, and that the BH Army simply did not allow any contact on the other side, no aid and assistance to come in or anything like that. So that was the only possibility open after more than 40 days. And I think that for the first time then, something was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, Mr. Jasak, co-operation with the Serbs in these enclaves that we've just mentioned, is that the consequence of goodwill on the part of the Croats, to co-operate with the Serbs against the Muslims, or was it a consequence of the circumstances in which the Muslim Army offensive actions brought them to, or is there something else?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was a necessary evil, if I can put it that way. The circumstances were such which led to that. There was no other way out.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jasak. Now let's move on to another area, Mostar and the moving out of people from flats. Now, to the best of your knowledge, the Main Staff of the HVO, were they in charge of seeing to law and order in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was not responsible for keeping public law and order.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us if the commander of the South-East Herzegovina Operations Zone was in charge of keeping public law and order in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that was not his responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALABURIC
utterances.text: To the best of your knowledge, Mr. Jasak, the representatives of the UNHCR, did they communicate with the civilian or the military authorities in Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think they co-operated with the civilian structures.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALABURIC
utterances.text: To the best of your knowledge, Mr. Jasak, the Main Staff, did it manage the flats that had been left void or were empty for any reason?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that the Main Staff had or managed any kind of flats or accommodation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let us now look at document 4D1303 in my small binder, 4D1303. It is a military report -- a report from the military police, dated June 1993. And in paragraph 5, it says there that on the 31st of May, 1993, the military police received an order that as of the 1st of June, 1993, in co-operation with the civilian police, it had to place a part of the town of Mostar under absolute control -- place under absolute control of the HVO-controlled part of the town of Mostar. "The order was issued because of a large number of criminal offences and the looting of flats especially at night." Now, Mr. Jasak, you told us about patrols and the introduction of a curfew. Now, did you have any knowledge to the effect that the authorities of Herceg-Bosna were trying to do everything in their power to fight crime, to punish the perpetrators, and to prevent looting?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would object to that question. That is very leading, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not a leading question. I'm just asking whether he had any knowledge of that. If he didn't, I won't pursue the matter. If he did, then I'll ask him to specify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. I am not going to rule on the Prosecution's objection, because this is a comment. Mr. Kruger, you, yourself, put this question right at the end when you asked the witness whether the HVO had done everything properly, so you addressed this issue. Therefore, the Defence is addressing the same topic. I don't see in what way this is a problem. You addressed the topic, and she is addressing the topic; in a different form, perhaps, but we're still talking about the same thing. What is important is that the witness answers the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Linked to this, well, the civilian police quite obviously could not have complete supervision over some groups that were -- well, there were Croats and Muslims. Whether they belonged to units, but they were in uniform. There were skirmishes and shooting around town; explosives were placed and so on. And quite obviously they tried to eliminate such behaviour and incidents.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jasak. We'll probably return to that in due course, but let's follow on from Ms. Senka Nozica's questions. She showed you document 4D36, which is a report from Arif Pasalic dated the 2nd of June, 1993 -- 2nd of May, 1993, sent to the Supreme Command Staff of the Armed Forces of the BH Army. And in that document, let me remind you, it was stated that: "A linkage with our people in the HVO was affected and that the bridge at Zitomislic should be taken control of, as well as two dominant elevations in Buna and positions facing Domanovici and the village of Stanojevici, and that Hodbine should be controlled." And then I'm going to skip over the next bit, because what we'd like to focus on is that: "The manpower from the HVO of Capljina had the task of taking control of the village of Tasovcici and the bridge at Capljina and that taking control of the town of Stolac was being planned with our people in the HVO." And then it goes on to say that mortars, 60 and 82-millimetre ones, had been positioned to open fire against the HVO, and so on and so forth. Now, my question to you is this, Mr. Jasak? Was this report compiled before or after the meeting in Jablanica? And you saw a short video about that, a five-minute video.

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was compiled before, because the other was the 4th of May, and this date here is the 2nd of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, if I remember correctly, at that meeting of the 4th of May, Sefer Halilovic asked General Petkovic a question. He said, Are we allies or enemies? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, Mr. Jasak, did the Prosecutor show you that Sefer Halilovic had informed General Petkovic that his first immediate subordinate, Arif Pasalic, had informed him of these plans for combat against the HVO in co-operation with the soldiers of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel slow down, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, Halilovic and Petkovic -- I mean Halilovic and Pasalic - I misspoke - in planning activities of this kind against the HVO and without informing the HVO about it, did they act as allies or potential -- a potential enemy army?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have an objection to this, Your Honour, that it's not in the record that there was, indeed, such an agreement, at least not with regard to this witness, that there was any such agreement between Pasalic -- or discussion between Pasalic and Halilovic, and therefore the question is inappropriate, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'd like to ask my learned friend to read who sent this report to whom. That's what I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Jasak, Pasalic's and Halilovic's acts, were they acts of allies or potential enemies?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was an act of potential enemies.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, staying with this document, Judge Trechsel asked you a question. He asked you about the ultimatum from the 1st Brigade sent to the BH Army, what kind of ultimatum it was, speaking about leaving Gubavica. And your answer to that question was as follows: You said that as far as you knew, it was entrance into the area of responsibility of another unit, that that's what that was about, and that the rule applied that without informing the commander of that other unit, you could not enter an area of responsibility of another unit. Did I understand you correctly to say that?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you understood me well. Regardless of whether it was a unit when some other HVO unit would come into the area of responsibility, the same would apply, the same rule would apply.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's now look at a few documents to see if your answers are reliable or not. And the first I'd like us to look at is 4D474, which is an order from Miljenko Lasic, the commander of the South-East Herzegovina Operative Zone, dated the 27th of March, 1993, in which, among other things, it says that it is prohibited to enter areas of responsibility of units without prior approval from the commander of that same unit and the commander of the operative zone: "And therefore I warn you --" and he goes on to say: "... and I oblige you to dislocate the units and their commands from the area of responsibility and the 1st HVO brigade, Knez Domagoj." This order was sent to the 4th Corps as well and to the BH Army brigade, the Bregava Brigade. Tell us, please, Witness, does this document confirm or deny your answer?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document confirms the answer I gave, because we can see quite clearly that this was sent to the -- to allies. Nothing was done behind their back. So what is asked for and how people should act was sent to the 4th Corps of the BH Army and the Bregava Brigade, which was the 42nd.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now let's look at the next document. P401 is the number. It is a list of people working in the Municipal Staff of the HVO of Mostar, dated the 22nd of August, 1992. You can see it up on your screen if you can't find it, and my question will be brief. Under point 9, point 9 of this document, on the list we see the independent Mostar battalion, and the commander is Arif Pasalic, or, rather, the next in command is Sulejman Budakovic. So Pasalic and Budakovic, were they staff of the Municipal Staff of the HVO in August 1992, as it says in this document here?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were, absolutely. They were under the command of the Municipal Staff of the HVO, in conformity with the previous decision taken by the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor showed you a document, 3D671 - listen to me carefully now - 3D671, and it was a SIS Mostar report of the 8th of July, 1992, about the situation in the municipality. And that report mentions that -- the alleged conflict between you, Mr. Jasak, and the chief of the battalion, the dispute between the two of you. And Judge Trechsel asked you a question in that regard. He asked you about the relationship between a commander and a chief or the commander and the chief, because his understanding up until that time was that a chief was, in fact, the commander. Now, your answer to that, Mr. Jasak, was as follows: You said you couldn't answer the question because in your battalion there was no chief of staff. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's look at the next document, P796 now, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I completely fail to grasp this last dialogue. There was no reference to any chief of staff in that document. There was the chief of the battalion and the commander of the battalion were mentioned there. If I had read "chief of staff," I admit my question would have been offendingly stupid. I ask stupid questions sometimes, but not that stupid.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, your question wasn't a stupid one at all. And had I considered it to be a stupid question, I wouldn't waste time on it. Now, I consider that your question was exceptionally important, because you had every reason to ask the question, because in the SIS document it truly did just say "chief." But in his answer, the witness, in fact, told you that a chief did not -- of staff did not exist in the battalion. So I wanted to use a document and indicate the difference between "chief of staff," because that's all that existed, unless he's a chief of some small organisational unit, but you can only have organisation in those terms. But if you don't need clarification between -- of the relationship between the chief of staff and the commander, then I can move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Just to be sure that I understand where we are: Witness, are you saying that when that document uses the term "chief," that is sloppy language, and what actually is meant is "chief of staff"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I assume that that was it, that a chief of staff of the battalion exists. And I understood you to ask about "chief" like "boss," like the number-one man.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if we've cleared that up, then I need not go into that document. I see that time is pressing, and I'm sure we'd all like us to complete this examination today, so let's move on to Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jasak, let's try and resolve the question of Konjic now. But before that, I'd like to thank Mr. Kruger for asking you a question from which the Prosecution position is clear, whereby the situation in Konjic cannot be understood if you don't know the situation in Prozor, what that was like. So then the same would hold true vice versa and would be applicable to other areas too. And I think that by that, we have dealt with the tu quoque Defence objections. The first document that I'd like us to look at, 4D139. 4D139 is the next document. Let's try and see what the relative finale of the clash over Konjic was for us better to understand some events that took place before that. Now, this document is already an exhibit, and tell us, please, Mr. Jasak, is this -- are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't had a chance to look at it yet, to see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you find your way in my binder? The orders go 2D, 3D, 4D, an order. 00139 is the number, 4D00139.

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am. And I know when it was written, and I know that the author of this document is my colleague Dinko Zebic, who originates from the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALABURIC
utterances.text: We have two parts here and Croatian villages listed in the Klis area and the Konjic area, which the Muslim Army took control of, and finally a note about the places in which fighting was still ongoing. Would that be a summary of this document, Mr. Jasak?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it would.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's take a look at document 4D1242 now, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. The document 4D139, I don't know whether it's been admitted or not, because this document gave rise to discussions before this Chamber. I don't know whether this document has been admitted or not. In the event that it has not been admitted, I have understood that you told us that this document had been drafted by one of your colleagues.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, I did say that. I said that it was compiled by Dinko Zebic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Based on all the information which the Main Staff had as regarded the military situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was compiled on the basis of everything that we had in Konjic. And I know that at this point in time when this was compiled, because I was present there, that the people personally who were expelled from the area provided certain information about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the record, this document was admitted on the 28th of January, 2009, according to the Legal Officer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: just said, this document is an exhibit already. But let's move on and look at 4D1242.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jasak, this is a map. I don't know if you've found it.

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALABURIC
utterances.text: It was prepared on the basis of the previous document, and it shows the villages taken control of by the Muslim Army and from which the Croats were expelled. Then we have marked places that were still under BH Army attack, and we also have the two Croatian enclaves that we mentioned earlier on. To the best of your knowledge, Mr. Jasak, does this map reflect the situation as you knew it?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does, because we can see the enclave here and the Neretvica River Valley, Kostajnica, and we see Turija, Zabrdje, and Zaslivlje near the town of Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, while we still have this document on our screens, I'm going to ask you something relating to General Petkovic's order dated the 18th of April, when he says that offensive operations should be stepped up in the direction of Klis. Is that the area around Kostajnica, which is in blue?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now let's look at the next document, which is 4D1241. The document is an exhibit already. It's an article taken from the 6th Corps of the BH Army Journal, which was published in 1994, the month of January. And I think in the central section there, it says literally as follows: "During the truce, the HVO planned an attack on the 16th of April, but our units, two days earlier, that is to say, on the 14th of April, by lightning attack, drove them down to Kostajnica, Vrci, and Ljesovina, where they remained for approximately three and a half months and then pulled out." Tell us, please, these localities, the ones mentioned here, do they have anything at all to do with Konjic?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they do. It's the Neretvica River Valley.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And is that the general area of Klis?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now let's take a look at the next document, which is P1803. And it's a report from SIS of the Rama Brigade from Prozor, dated the 14th of April, 1993. And in section 5 or paragraph 5, it says that certain members of the BH Army -- let me correct the date. The 4th of April is the date. Members of the BH Army, as I was saying, were refusing the call-up to come up to the front-line facing the Serbs, and organised themselves and left to go to Here, Kute, and Scipe, and there they attacked the HVO units and looted Croatian villages which had been left empty. Now, in this courtroom, we heard -- have heard of these villages, these three villages. Now, can you tell us why those three villages in the Prozor municipality have significance?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are three villages which are predominantly Muslim and which are located along the borders of -- or between the borders of Prozor and Konjic municipalities. And forces were brought in there from the area south of Sarajevo, towards Vakuf, and that's from where the attacks were launched towards the Neretvica River Valley and the Croatian villages located in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now look at the next document, please, which is 4D91. And it's a combat report from a commander in the Muslim Army for the 24th of April, 1993. You can listen to me. We don't have time to look for the document now. Just listen to me. It says that for the 25th of April, the plan was to continue activities throughout the front-line and to take control of Vrci and Budisna Ravan. Tell us, please, Mr. Jasak, to the best of your knowledge, Sefer Halilovic, at the meeting in Jablanica on the 4th of May, did he inform the HVO representatives about the fact that his army was planning to continue its activities throughout the front and to take control of these two localities which were inhabited by the Croatians?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, to the best of my knowledge, he did not inform General Petkovic about that. He did not respect the truce, either, which had been signed previously in Zenica, because he and General Petkovic signed a truce -- an agreement for a truce on the 20th. No, I mean the 24th. I meant to say the 24th, not the 20th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, in your opinion, Mr. Jasak, Sefer Halilovic, did he act as an ally or as a potential or actual enemy?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he was an actual enemy in those parts already at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's look at the next document now, please, which is 4D454. And they are the minutes from a meeting held on the 20th of March, 1993, which my colleague Mr. Kruger showed you. What I'd like to focus on is point 7, in which it says that full control of the area should be ensured along the axis of Jablanica-Kute-Here-Scipe, and that the forces should be tied in with the forces of the armies in the neighbouring municipalities. Let's take a look at the next document, which is under seal. IC1124 is the number. On this document, which is under seal, paragraph 5 sets out the tasks of [indiscernible] 5 of the 20th of March, and paragraph 7 -- well, the order under item 7 that I read out earlier on. We don't have the map on our screens yet.

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Once we all have the map on our screens, would you tell us the following: If this axis, Jablanica-Here-Kute-Scipe on the right bank, if you want to link it up with the neighbouring municipality, which territory is it that the Muslim army needs to take control of? Just use your felt-tip pen and draw lines across this territory to show us.

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Up here [indicates] -- it's gone off the screen. Up here we have Here [indicates]. It's gone off the screen again. It's back. Here-Kute-Scipe up here [indicates], but now the pen isn't working.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Just cross over the territory. Can we have the map shown as it stands? Now, Mr. Jasak, these three lines finish at the point of these three villages? "Jablanica" is Jablanica municipality; Kute-Here-Scipe, is Prozor municipality; and to the right of the line, Jablanica-Kute-Here-Scipe, you have Konjic municipality. And this is where --

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see the lake down there, Jablanica Lake, and the Neretvica River Valley, and that's the Croatian area.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And now to the right of those lines, the Muslim Army wants to gain full control and link up the municipalities of Konjic and Prozor, which territory does it need to take control of?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It needs to take control of the territory Boksevica-Neretvica Valley, all that general area, which is where the HVO was, which meant that the HVO needed to be routed, defeated.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. Draw in that territory, please.

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't. This pen won't write on the screen. I start writing and the map disappears. No, no good.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we place the map on the ELMO and have the witness mark it there? Mr. Jasak -- or, Your Honours, shall we continue tomorrow morning, because I see that it's time for the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Nozica or, rather, Ms. Alaburic, how long do you need to complete your redirect?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think I need some 10 minutes, if we don't have technical problems like this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I made a circle around the Neretvica Valley and all the villages in that general area, so these circles here towards Konjic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Nozica [as interpreted], you have 10 minutes. Because they have another hearing here, so I can make an effort to extend an extra 10 minutes. So please complete in order to avoid for everyone to have to come back tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, I'll do that much. Let us just describe what the witness has drawn.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, you marked in the territory which the Muslim army should take control of in order to accomplish the task of linking up the municipalities of Prozor and Konjic, complete control over those municipalities; right? Is that what you've drawn there?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, could you sign the map, and may we have an IC number for the map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you please give a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the marked portion of this map shall be given Exhibit IC01167. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Jasak, if we recall the VOS document and the subsequent events, did the Muslim army accomplish its goal, the goal that it designed on the 20th of March, 1993?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did accomplish its goal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In the next document - you needn't look at it, just listen to me - it's P1872, it's an order from Miljenko Lasic dated the 14th of April, shown to you by my learned friend Mr. Kruger. It speaks about the moving of artillery pieces to Sovicka Vrata and Risovac, those two localities. When we say that artillery pieces need to be transferred to a new location, does that mean that they were somewhere else and then had to be brought to this new location?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it means, that they were elsewhere and needed to be transferred to this other place.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now let's see why Sovicka Vrata and Risovac are mention. Document 2D246 is the one I'd like us to look at next. The other locality that I mentioned is Risovac. Now, in this document, it's an order from the Command of the 44th Mountain Brigade from Jablanica. From this document, we can see, if we look at, say, paragraphs 5 and 6, that forces needed to be brought in to take control of positions at Risovac and Sovicka Vrata and prevent the possibility of the HVO bringing in reinforcements from other areas. Tell us, please, Mr. Jasak, as you understand matters, the arrival of the artillery pieces in the Risovac and Sovicka Vrata area, did they have anything to do with the previous combat activities of the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does, and it's a reaction to the former activities of the BH Army, and it was exclusively for assistance to the area that we looked at a moment ago and that I encircled in the Neretvica River Valley.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALABURIC
utterances.text: P1915, the next document, is a report from Zeljko Siljeg, dated the 16th of April, 1993. And in that report, among other things, it says that a wire connection with the Herceg Stjepan Command has been established. What I'm interested in is paragraph 12 of the report, which says that a detailed and precise report is required on the situation, and precise demands for action. And he's asking this from the Command of the Herceg Stjepan Brigade. Tell us, please, what brigade is that Herceg Stjepan Brigade?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the Konjic Brigade which was under siege, in an encirclement. And we saw the call for help earlier on, so they want to act upon that, but then they don't know what the situation is, specifically, because they don't have all the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, from this report, does it follow that the Zeljko Siljeg units acted upon the request made from the Konjic Brigade?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and you can see that from the previous request by the Command of the Konjic Brigade when he asks for assistance from all sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And now the last document I'd like you to comment on is P2760. It is a piece of information or proposal from Zarko Keza, dated the 14th of --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch the month.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Jasak, you told us -- let me repeat the date. The 14th of June, 1993, is the date. You told us that the document was issued in a situation that was an extraordinary one. So apart from the two Croatian enclaves in the Konjic municipality, was there any single patch of territory in that municipality where there was still Croatian inhabitants?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't have any information to the effect that anybody -- any Croats had stayed on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, up until that time, tell us, please, the Muslim Army, did it take control of Travnik, Novi Travnik, and Kakanj in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did, and because we're dealing with mid-June. That's the mid-June period.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, at that time, did you know about the BH Army plans at all that from Central Bosnia and the Neretva River Valley they moved towards the sea?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did have knowledge about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Was this alarming news or improbable news?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were absolutely alarming. It was alarming information. And I said yesterday that information of that kind led to proposals of this kind for very difficult situations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, this document from your immediate superior, he proposes that the BH Army -- the term "BH Army" should no longer be used, but that the term "Muslim forces" should be used in future, so I'd like to enforce the Sanction system for us to take a look at paragraph 2 of the appeals judgement in the Blaskic trial to see what the Court had to say and what this Tribunal called the army of the Muslims of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It says the following: [In English] "The events giving rise to this appeal took place during the conflict between the Croatian Defence Council and the Bosnian Muslim Army in the Lasva Valley ..." [Interpretation] Et cetera. Now, to the best of your knowledge, Mr. Jasak, at the end of June 1993, was it correct to call the army led by Rasim Delic the Muslim Army or the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The correct way was to call it the Muslim Army, because that's what, in fact, it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My last question, but for that may we move into private session. And this will, indeed, be my last question.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In open session, we have extended the time here. I apologise to all and everyone. I'd like to thank you, Witness, for having come to The Hague at the request of the Petkovic Defence team. I wish you a safe journey home. We shall meet again on Monday, the 8th of February, at quarter past 2.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 8th day of February, 2010, at 2.15 p.m. 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.01 p.m.,
